web.description:
# Qwen3-Coder-Next Technical Report
###### Abstract
Across agent-centric benchmarks including SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench, Qwen3-Coder-Next achieves competitive performance relative to its active parameter count.

## 5 Experiments
### 5.1 Agentic Evaluation
##### Setting.
We evaluate Qwen3-Coder-Next on three SWE benchmarks, SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#bib.bib361)), SWE-Bench Multilingual (Yang et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#bib.bib368)), and SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#bib.bib2)), and a command-line interface (CLI) task, TerminalBench 2.0 (Merrill et al., [2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#bib.bib10)).

##### SWE Coding Tasks.
[Table˜3](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#S5.T3) reports results on SWE-Bench Verified across three agent scaffolds. Specifically, it achieves scores of 70.6% with SWE-Agent, 71.1% with MiniSWE-Agent, and 71.3% with OpenHands.

[Table˜4](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#S5.T4) presents results on SWE-Bench Multilingual, which evaluates repository-level bug fixing across multiple programming languages, as well as the more challenging SWE-Bench Pro benchmark.

##### Command-line Interface tasks.
[Table˜5](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00729v1#S5.T5) shows the results on Terminal Bench 2.0, Qwen3-Coder-Next demonstrates consistent performance across multiple TerminalBench 2.0 environments, including XML- and JSON-based tool schemas as well as different agent scaffolds.

## Background
SWE-bench, introduced by Jimenez et al. in their seminal paper [“Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?”](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.06770), has emerged as a prominent benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering contexts.

The benchmark comprises 500 tasks, each executed within an isolated Docker container. The success of a model’s solution is determined by running unit tests against the generated patch.

A notable complexity of SWE-bench lies in its dual evaluation of both the agentic harness and the underlying foundation model. Additionally, the benchmark’s computational requirements make it resource-intensive to reproduce results.

Models that perform well on SWE-bench Verified tend to be proficient with bash and standard command-line tools for code navigation and editing.

There is also a clear trend that closed-source models perform better on SWE-bench Verified than open-source models. The clearest performance differences appear among tasks that take between 15 minutes and 1 hour to complete. Models that perform well on these tasks tend to score higher overall on the benchmark.

## Methodology
We use the SWE-bench Verified subset of the dataset. SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated section of the SWE-bench dataset released by OpenAI in August 2024. Each task in the split has been carefully reviewed and validated by human experts, resulting in a curated set of 500 high-quality test cases from the original benchmark.
